questions.question: Explain how an earthquake is generated, distinguishing clearly between focus and epicentre, and account for the influence of focus depth on the damage caused.
questions.expected_answer: Tectonic forces load rock with strain while friction holds a fault locked. The rock deforms elastically and stores that energy, sometimes for centuries. When the accumulated strain exceeds the strength of the rock or the friction holding it, the fault slips and the rock snaps back toward its original shape, releasing the stored energy as seismic vibrations — elastic rebound. The FOCUS, or hypocentre, is the point within the crust where the rupture begins and energy is first released; the EPICENTRE is the point on the surface directly above the focus, where shaking is usually strongest. Focus depth is classified as shallow (0–70 km), intermediate (70–300 km) and deep (300–700 km). Shallow-focus earthquakes are by far the most destructive, because the energy is released close to the surface and little of it is absorbed by intervening rock before it reaches buildings; deep-focus events, which occur only along subduction zones, arrive at the surface much weakened.

questions.question: Distinguish between the Richter and Mercalli scales, and explain why an earthquake of magnitude 7 is far more serious than the numbers alone suggest.
questions.expected_answer: The Richter scale measures MAGNITUDE — the energy released at the focus, calculated from seismograph amplitude corrected for distance. It gives one value per earthquake, regardless of what happens at the surface, and has no upper limit. The Mercalli scale measures INTENSITY — the observed effects at a particular place — on a scale of I to XII in Roman numerals, so one earthquake produces many Mercalli values, high near the epicentre and lower further away, and varying with local ground conditions, focus depth and building quality. The Richter scale is logarithmic: each whole number step means ten times the ground movement and roughly thirty-two times the energy released. A magnitude 7 is therefore two steps above a magnitude 5, which is ten times ten, or one hundred times the ground movement, and about thirty-two times thirty-two, roughly one thousand times the energy. Describing that difference as 'slightly stronger' is the classic error; it is a difference of a thousandfold in energy.

questions.question: Two earthquakes of similar magnitude occur in different countries, but one causes a few hundred deaths and the other more than a hundred thousand. Explain the factors that account for this, and describe the strategies used to reduce earthquake impact.
questions.expected_answer: The difference is vulnerability rather than geology. Building quality and the enforcement of earthquake-resistant codes matter most, because it is collapsing structures that kill people; densely populated cities close to the epicentre multiply casualties; wealth determines whether a country can fund monitoring networks, trained rescue services, hospitals with backup power and rebuilding; the time of day affects how many people are indoors and asleep; and local ground conditions matter greatly, since loose sediment or reclaimed land amplifies shaking while bedrock transmits far less of it. Reduction rests on preparedness rather than prediction, because although geologists can map high-risk zones and monitor foreshocks, ground tilt, groundwater and radon gas, nobody can name a date. Engineering measures include base isolators of rubber and steel that let the ground move while the building stays comparatively still, cross-bracing, flexible frames, lighter roofs and foundations anchored to bedrock. Planning measures include land-use zoning that keeps hospitals and schools off active faults and unstable ground, and building codes that are genuinely inspected. Community measures include regular drills, the drop-cover-and-hold-on routine, emergency kits and family meeting points, supported by seismometer networks that give seconds of warning and, on coasts, tsunami warning systems.
